description: We’re a complete team with full-stack web development experience.
summary: NASA FIRMS records fire hotspots from two kinds of instrument. VIIRS, flying since 2012, finds about 3.4 times as many hotspots as MODIS. Simply adding the two fakes a jump: Greece goes from 2,524 hotspots in 2011 to 9,245 in 2012. HOTSPOT measures the MODIS-to-VIIRS factor on the years both flew, separately for day and night and for the fire season. It gives every Greek hotspot since 2000 a weight in NOAA-20 units, NOAA-20 being the satellite that continues now that S-NPP has stopped. Pick any area and dates and you get a month-by-year calendar against normal, a plain headline sentence, rankings, a trend test and downloads. Every estimate shows its arithmetic. Tested blind on years the fit never saw, whole years came within 7.8%. The finding: August 2007 had about 11,606 hotspots on the VIIRS scale (range 8,554 to 14,659), more than August 2021 (6,893) or August 2023 (5,736).
details:
What it does and how it works

HOTSPOT (https://hotspots.gr) turns NASA's two satellite fire records into one consistent record for Greece, from November 2000 to today.

NASA FIRMS publishes fire hotspots from MODIS (1 km pixels, since 2000) and from VIIRS (375 m pixels, since 2012). The two instruments differ in spatial resolution, sensitivity and observation schedule. As a result, VIIRS finds about 3.4 times as many hotspots as MODIS for the same fires (37,448 against 10,978 in Greece, 2012 to 2019). Simply adding the two fakes a jump: Greece goes from 2,524 hotspots in 2011 to 9,245 in 2012, when only the instrument changed.

HOTSPOT fixes this in five steps:

  1. Clean. Keep vegetation fires, agricultural burns included. Remove fixed industrial heat sources and low-confidence detections.
  2. Never add satellites that see the same thing. Terra and Aqua pass at different times of day, so we add them. S-NPP and NOAA-20 see nearly the same fires, so we use one at a time.
  3. Measure the MODIS-to-VIIRS factor ourselves on 2012 to 2019, the years both flew before the MODIS orbits drifted. It is measured separately for day and night, and for the fire season against the rest of the year. The Terra-only years before July 2002 get their own factor.
  4. Link S-NPP to NOAA-20 with a measured factor of 1.04. NOAA-20 is the satellite that continues now that S-NPP has stopped.
  5. Give every hotspot a weight in NOAA-20 units. Any area a user draws is summed exactly, and every download is itself harmonized data.

In the app, a user:

  • picks an area by drawing a shape, by typing a point and a radius, or with a preset (North Evia 2021, Evros 2023, All Greece), then picks a date range
  • gets a month-by-year calendar heatmap with a "normal year" row (the median of each calendar month), year totals, a "difference from normal" view and a raw view
  • reads a plain headline sentence and a "this month so far" card against the same days of earlier years
  • sees rankings and the peak season, a yearly trend with a Mann-Kendall test, and a seasonal chart
  • clicks a month to see its hotspots on the map
  • downloads the calendar as CSV and as an image, and the hotspots as CSV with their weights

A "Method and proof" page shows the method, seven proofs as charts, and the limits. A GitHub Actions job adds new NOAA-20 data from NASA's FIRMS API every day.

Benefits

  • One scale for 26 years. A fire year before 2012 can finally be compared with a recent one.
  • Every number can be traced. Hover over any estimated month and HOTSPOT shows its arithmetic. For August 2007: 3,052 MODIS detections × 3.80 = 11,606 (range 8,554 to 14,659).
  • Honest about uncertainty. Every estimate before 2012 carries a measured range, and the page lists what the record cannot answer.
  • Fast, for anyone. Your own area against its history in under a minute, with no satellite knowledge needed.
  • Reusable. An open dataset of 153,804 weighted hotspots, a public web address for the calendar, and open code (Apache-2.0) with rebuild steps.

Intended impact

HOTSPOT is for the audience the challenge names: early warning and emergency responders, scientists, firefighters and civilians. It shows history, not a forecast. It supports three decisions:

  1. Planning: when does the dangerous season normally start and end here? For All Greece, July to October.
  2. Alert: is this month unusual for this area?
  3. After a fire: how does this event compare with the worst on record here, across the change of instrument?

It is also timely. S-NPP stopped delivering data on 2 November 2026, and the MODIS satellites are drifting. A record built on NOAA-20 keeps 26 years of history usable after the older sensors are gone.

Tools, languages and software

  • Languages: Python 3.13 (data pipeline), TypeScript (website), SQL (database functions)
  • Data pipeline: pandas, SciPy, Requests, psycopg 3, pytest
    • NASA FIRMS MODIS C6.1 and VIIRS 375 m (S-NPP, NOAA-20), plus the FIRMS Area API
    • Copernicus EMS activations EMSR527 and EMSR686, and EFFIS burned area
    • Natural Earth; OpenStreetMap
  • AI: The code was written with Claude Code, under the team's direction and review. 
  • Hardware: none beyond the team's own computers.

How it is creative

  • A finding nobody could make before. Was 2007 worse than 2021 or 2023? MODIS counted 2007 and VIIRS counted the later years, so their numbers could not be compared. On one scale, August 2007 had about 11,606 hotspots, against 6,893 in August 2021 and 5,736 in August 2023. Even the low end of 2007's range is above both.
  • A glass box, not a black box. Every estimate shows its arithmetic, and a raw-versus-harmonized switch shows the fake 2012 jump appear and disappear for the user's own area.
  • The proof is inside the product. All seven proofs are on the same site as the tool.
  • A correction on every single hotspot, not on a coarse grid. Any shape is exact, and the download is harmonized data.
  • New measured ratios for a Mediterranean country. S-NPP finds 2.63 hotspots per MODIS hotspot by day and 4.96 by night in the fire season, and 3.36 and 11.52 the rest of the year. We found none published, though we did not search exhaustively.

Factors the team considered

  • Scientific validity.
    • A blind test: fit on 2012 to 2016, predict 2017 to 2019. Whole years came within 7.8% on average, fire-season months within 26.3%.
    • Day-by-day checks of the Evros 2023 and North Evia 2021 fires against the Copernicus burned-area maps.
    • A rank correlation of 0.70 with EFFIS burned area, 2006 to 2025.
    • A monthly correlation of 0.998 at the NOAA-20 join.
    • Tests of what the factor is made of, and of the obvious alternative, a common grid. A grid only lowers the ratio from 3.41 to between 2.62 and 2.87, so it cannot replace the factor.
    • adding the sensors together
    • a common grid
    • fitting on years after the MODIS drift
    • the VIIRS 750 m product as the main source (named as a next step)
    • the mean as "normal": we use the median, so one extreme year cannot move it
    • Values before 2012 are estimates, and fires MODIS never saw cannot be recovered.
    • Small areas vary more than the whole country.
    • Hotspots are not burned area.
    • The newest months are provisional.
    • We make no claim about 2001, the shaky first year.
  • Accessibility. A colour-blind-safe colour ramp, patterns as well as colour, numbers on hover, keyboard focus or tap, a table view for screen readers, and a phone layout.
  • Scope and reliability. One country done completely rather than the world half-done. Proof charts are files inside the website, so they show even if the database is down. The data updates itself every day.
  • Next steps: more Mediterranean countries (the pipeline takes the country as a setting), the VIIRS 750 m product as a bridge, and an alert when an area goes above its normal.
